In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the induction of tyrosine transminase by glucagon is not sensitive to 5-azacitidine and that the induction of the enzyme by hydrocorti- sone is sensitive to the drug, but only after the initial glucagon-mediated induction of the transaminase.

the glucocorticoid-mediated induction of tyrosine transminase requires the presence of a specific protein component which is not synthesized in the presence of 5-azacitidine and which is induced by glucagon (or cyclic AMP).

the initial induction of the enzyme by glucagon or its second messenger, cyclic AMP, is independent of RNA synthesis and does not involve a common component with the hydrocortisome-mediated induction, whereas the subsequent hydrocortisose-mediated induction is dependent on RNA synthesis and does involve a common component, presumably at the transcriptional level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

glucocorticoids induce the enzyme via a mechanism which involves the transcription of new mRNA, whereas the induction by glucagon (or cyclic AMP) occurs via a post-transcriptional mechanism, which involves the activation of a pre-existing mRNA.
the glucocorticoid-mediated induction of hepatic enzymes is a two-step process, involving a common component, and is not mediated by a glucocorticoid-receptor complex.
the initial induction of tyrosine transaminate by hydrocorti- sone and glucagon is independent of RNA synthesis and is not sensitive to inhibition by azacytidine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the glucagon-mediated induction of tyrosine transaminiase, like that of hydrocortisine, is dependent upon the synthesis of a protein factor.
the glucagon-mediated induction of tyrosine transminase is not dependent on the synthesis of new mRNA.
